Amazon SDE Interview Experience 2026 | Seattle Onsite, Team Match, Coding & GenAI Questions - DEV Community

I finished my Amazon SDE interview at the end of April and received my offer on May 5th. There was also a stressful moment in between: my original team suddenly lost headcount, so I had to go through a new team matching process after passing the interviews.

Instead of writing a traditional round-by-round interview log, I want to share the things that actually surprised me, the questions that caught me off guard, and the lessons I only understood after the process was over.

## Amazon SDE Interview Timeline

- November: Applied for Amazon SDE position
- Early March: Received OA invitation
- April 1: Received onsite interview invitation
- April 20: Seattle onsite interview
- April 22: Received email saying I passed interviews, but original team no longer had HC
- April 28: Matched with a new team and scheduled HM call
- May 1: HM interview
- May 5: Offer received

The most stressful moment was definitely the April 22 email. Passing the interviews but losing the team because of headcount was a strange feeling. Fortunately, the team matching process only took about a week.

## All Three Interviewers Were Indian — Does It Matter?

A lot of people worry about interviewer background, especially accents. In my case, all three interviewers were Indian. But after going through the entire process, my biggest takeaway was:

Their follow-up questions were very reasonable. If you cannot explain something clearly, you simply cannot explain it — it has nothing to do with the interviewer's accent.

They focused heavily on details, tradeoffs, and the reasoning behind my decisions.

## Round 1: Hiring Manager Interview

The first interviewer was the most extroverted one. Before the official interview started, we spent several minutes casually chatting.

### Behavioral Questions

The behavioral questions were standard Amazon-style questions:

- Tell me about a time you had a tight deadline.
- How did you debug a difficult issue?
- How do you use AI tools in your daily development?

The AI question was especially interesting because it has become a much more common topic recently. The interviewer followed up with:

"How do you reduce AI hallucinations?"

I answered based on my real experience using Copilot, including:

- Reviewing AI-generated code carefully
- Identifying situations where AI output is unreliable
- Using tests and documentation to validate suggestions

If you have never actually used AI coding tools, this question is difficult to answer naturally.

### Coding Question

The coding problem was not from LeetCode. Amazon created a business scenario:

Given the latest 1,000 orders, determine whether a new order was created by an abusive user.

The algorithm itself was easy, around LeetCode Easy level. The difficult part was that the requirements were vague.

I spent around five minutes clarifying requirements before coding. The implementation itself only took about ten minutes.

My biggest lesson:

For Amazon business-style coding questions, clarification is often more important than coding speed.

## Round 2: Applied Scientist Interview + Shadow Interviewer

The second interviewer was an Applied Scientist. There was also a remote shadow interviewer in the meeting.

At first, I thought the shadow interviewer was only observing. However, he actually asked follow-up questions later.

This was something I had rarely seen mentioned in previous interview experiences.

### Behavioral Questions

The behavioral questions included:

- A time you failed and what you learned
- A time you gained someone's trust
- A time you improved an existing system
- A time you learned something new

The conversation felt a little messy because the interviewer jumped between topics, and my answers were not as structured as I wanted.

### Coding Question

The coding problem:

Given a list of unordered timestamps and a maximum gap value, two timestamps belong to the same interval if they are within the allowed gap. Return all valid intervals.

The solution was straightforward:

- Sort timestamps
- Scan linearly
- Merge intervals

After I finished, the shadow interviewer asked:

"How can you optimize this further?"

I got stuck because I believed my solution was already optimal.

The lesson:

Shadow interviewers are not just observers. They may challenge your solution too.

## Round 3: Hiring Manager Interview — Almost Pure Conversation

The third interviewer was another Hiring Manager. Surprisingly, there was almost no technical content.

The conversation focused on:

- Why I transferred schools
- What CS courses I was taking
- My favorite CS subject
- The business logic behind my startup experience
- My experience with GenAI

The entire interview lasted around 40 minutes, including three questions from me.

The funny thing:

The interviewer became more and more expressionless toward the end. I thought I failed.

Four days later, I received the offer.

Do not judge your result based on the interviewer's facial expression.

## Amazon SDE Interview FAQ

### Was coding on a whiteboard or computer?

I wrote code on a whiteboard in the meeting room. I brought my laptop, but we did not use it.

### Did the HM evaluation call include coding?

No. It was purely conversational.

### Was there resume deep dive?

Yes. Most behavioral questions were actually deep dives into my resume experiences.

### How long did it take to confirm the interview schedule?

About two days.

### What GenAI questions were asked?

Mainly:

- How do you use AI tools?
- How do you reduce AI hallucinations?

## What I Would Prepare Differently Next Time

Looking back, there were several things I underestimated.

### 1. Coding Questions Were Business Scenarios, Not LeetCode

All three coding rounds were custom Amazon-style business problems. The difficulty was not high, but the requirements were unclear.

Clarification skills mattered more than memorizing algorithms.

### 2. GenAI Has Become a Real Interview Topic

Two rounds asked about AI usage. Interviewers were not only asking whether you use AI, but whether you understand its limitations.

### 3. Behavioral Preparation Still Matters

The first two rounds heavily focused on behavioral questions. However, my third HM round was almost completely casual conversation.

### 4. Passing Interviews Does Not Always Mean Immediate Offer

Team availability and headcount can still affect the final result. My team match experience was a reminder that the process is not always linear.

## Final Preparation Advice

The two things I was least prepared for were:

- "How do you reduce AI hallucinations?"
- "Can you optimize your solution further?"

These are not questions you can solve by grinding LeetCode.

For AI questions, you need real experience using AI tools and understanding their failure modes.

For optimization questions, you need practice explaining tradeoffs after reaching a standard solution.

During my preparation, I used InterviewShow for Amazon mock interviews. The biggest improvement came from repeatedly being pushed with questions like "Can you optimize this?" until thinking about alternatives became automatic.

When the real interview happened, I was much calmer because I had already experienced that pressure during practice.

## Conclusion

Amazon SDE interviews are not just about solving coding problems. The interviewers care about how you clarify requirements, explain decisions, handle ambiguity, and think about engineering tradeoffs.

Good luck to everyone preparing for Amazon interviews. Hope everyone gets the offer they want.

# It's been three months since I joined Amazon as an SDE2, and the learning experience has been incredible. The scale of engineering problems, the people I've worked with, and the engineering culture … | Anusha Kandagal · LinkedIn · 2026-07-26

**Anusha Kandagal**: Software development engineer 2 (L5) at Amazon with 5 years 3 months of experience. Previous roles include Software development engineer III at Walmart Global Tech India, Software Development Engineer -2 at Amadeus, and Software development Engineer - 1 at Amadeus. Based in Greater Bengaluru Area [IN].

---

It's been three months since I joined Amazon as an SDE2, and the learning experience has been incredible. The scale of engineering problems, the people I've worked with, and the engineering culture have all been amazing.

Many have reached out about my interview experience, so here’s a summary of my journey—from application to offer. I've also attached a detailed LeetCode discussion post for those preparing for Amazon SDE-2 interviews.

📝 Application Process
I applied through Amazon's online job portal and received a HackerRank assessment link after my application was shortlisted.

💻 Online Assessment (OA)
The OA included coding, work simulation, and work-style assessments. Amazon is evolving the assessment format to incorporate AI-assisted development experiences, so candidates should expect slight variations depending on the hiring cycle.

🏢 Interview Structure (4 Rounds)
The interview process evaluates candidates across four pillars:
- DSA / Problem Solving
- System & Software Design (LLD/HLD)
- Amazon Leadership Principles
- Gen AI Fluency

- Round 1 – In-Person: DSA / Problem Solving.
- Round 2 – In-Person: System Design (LLD/HLD).
- Round 3 – In-Person: System Design (LLD/HLD).
- Round 4 (Bar Raiser) – Virtual.

Some key highlights:
- All four rounds contribute to the final hiring decision.
- The first three rounds are conducted onsite, while the Bar Raiser was virtual in my case.
- Interviewers are usually prospective teammates, providing insight into the team and its engineering culture.
- I was assigned a lunch buddy from the hiring team, offering an informal look into their projects and what I could potentially work on.

📌 What's Covered in the Detailed LeetCode Post?
I've detailed:
- Exact coding and system design questions from each round.
- Leadership Principles and Gen AI-related questions asked.
- OA details and preparation tips.

👉 https://lnkd.in/dAcPZyY9

I hope this helps anyone preparing for a similar role.

# Amazon SDE II / SDE III Interview Guide

5 rounds · 5-6 hours total · Updated 2026

Rounds

5

Total Time

5-6 hours

Topics

4

## The Amazon interview process, round by round

1. Online assessment

70-min OA: 2 coding problems plus a work-simulation.

2. Recruiter/hiring manager call

30-45 min: leadership principles preview + role fit.

3. Onsite loop: 4-5 rounds

Each round: coding + 2 Leadership Principle behavioral questions using STAR.

4. Bar Raiser round

One round conducted by trained interviewer from outside the team with veto power.

5. Debrief

Team + BR align on level and hire/no-hire.

## Topics Amazon tests

Amazon Leadership Principles (16)Coding (BFS/DFS, trees, DP)Object-oriented designSystem design (SDE III+)

## How to prep for Amazon

- Every round = STAR stories tied to a Leadership Principle
- Have 2 stories per principle ready
- Bar Raiser is trained to spot 'raise the bar' hires
- OA cheating is aggressively detected — do it clean

## Amazon compensation (2026)

SDE II: $190K-$ 260K TC · SDE III: $290K-$ 400K TC · Principal: $500K+ TC

Total comp includes base, target bonus, and 4-year vesting equity annualized.

## FAQs

How many rounds is the Amazon interview?

5 rounds, 5-6 hours total across recruiter screen, technical rounds, and behavioral.

What topics does Amazon test on?

Amazon Leadership Principles (16), Coding (BFS/DFS, trees, DP), Object-oriented design, System design (SDE III+).

What does a Amazon SDE II / SDE III make?

SDE II: $190K-$ 260K TC · SDE III: $290K-$ 400K TC · Principal: $500K+ TC

How hard is the Amazon interview?

Selectivity varies by level; typical pass rate is 3-8% at the onsite stage. Preparation on Amazon Leadership Principles (16) and Coding (BFS/DFS, trees, DP) is the highest ROI.

# Recently, I interviewed for an Amazon SDE2 role. One interesting change I noticed was in the Online Assessment (OA): in addition to the usual DSA and Leadership Principles (LP) questions, it now … | Rajani Tak · LinkedIn · 2026-07-28

**Rajani Tak**: Back End Developer at BeeHyv Software for 11 months with 6 years 3 months of total professional experience. Previous roles include Senior Software Engineer (Backend-SDE2) at Sashel, Full Stack Engineer at Tietoevry, and Research Development Project Engineer at Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay. Based in Hyderabad, Telangana, India [IN].

---

Recently, I interviewed for an [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) SDE2 role. One interesting change I noticed was in the Online Assessment (OA): in addition to the usual DSA and Leadership Principles (LP) questions, it now also includes a bug-fixing task in an existing source code repository.
The interview process consisted of four rounds after the OA:
• Round 1: Data Structures & Algorithms (any programming language)
• Round 2: Low-Level Design (LLD)
• Round 3: High-Level Design (HLD)
• Round 4: Bar Raiser (can be of DSA or LLD)
In each interview round, around 15 minutes were dedicated to Leadership Principles (LP) questions.
Although I didn't make it through to the end, the experience was incredibly valuable. It gave me a much better understanding of [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon)'s interview expectations and highlighted areas where I can continue improving. Overall, it was a great learning experience, and I'm looking forward to applying these lessons in future interviews.

I also got a chance to interview at [FactSet](https://linkedin.com/company/factset) & [BlueFlag Security](https://linkedin.com/company/blueflag-security);
For [FactSet](https://linkedin.com/company/factset), there were three rounds for the SDE Backend role. The first two rounds were more focused on OOPS, JAVA & DSA, with a bit of resume-based & the last was managerial.

For [BlueFlag Security](https://linkedin.com/company/blueflag-security), there were three rounds for the SDE role: the first two were System Design & last one was Java (or any language in which you are proficient) & one managerial round.

I'm currently in the interview pipeline with a few other companies as well. Once those processes conclude, I'll share interview experiences for each as well. Hopefully, they'll help others preparing for similar roles by giving them a clearer idea of what to expect.
Wishing everyone who's interviewing the very best—keep learning and keep improving!

# To crack Amazon SDE 2, I focused on DSA, LLD, HLD and Leadership Principles. | Siddharth Singh · LinkedIn · 2026-07-28

**Siddharth Singh**: SDE 2 at Amazon for 5 months with 4 years 1 month of total professional experience. Previous roles include SDE 2 at Goldman Sachs, Software Engineer at Wells Fargo, and Program Associate at Wells Fargo. Based in Bengaluru, Karnataka, India [IN].

---

To crack [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) SDE 2, I focused on DSA, LLD, HLD and Leadership Principles.

Last week I shared the DSA and LP breakdown and hundreds of you commented asking for LLD and HLD.

So here it is.

LLD

Don't start with problems directly.

Revise design patterns first. All in one videos on YouTube cover this well.

Understand the patterns before jumping into questions.

Then watch 3-4 interview question videos to understand how to approach LLD in a real interview setting.

Then practice with ChatGPT acting as the interviewer. Give it the problem. Ask it to question your approach, push back, ask for extensions.

That discomfort in practice makes the real interview feel familiar.

Recently asked questions worth covering:

→ Vending Machine
→ Parking Lot
→ Splitwise
→ Rate Limiter, understand Token Bucket Algorithm specifically
→ LRU Cache
→ Chess Game
→ WhatsApp Messenger
→ IRCTC Booking System, focus on the booking module
→ Movie Booking System
→ [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) Locker

These repeat. Take them seriously.

HLD

Revise core fundamentals first, don't jump to questions without this.

→ Caching
→ API Design
→ Database Fundamentals
→ Distributed Systems and Microservices
→ Asynchronous Communication
→ Architectural Patterns
→ System Design Tradeoffs

Then practice recently asked [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) HLD questions.

3 things that actually made a difference in my HLD rounds:
Discuss tradeoffs always.

[Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) specifically evaluates how you decide between options not just what you chose but why. Every design choice should come with "I chose this over X because..."

Learn DynamoDB.

It's [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon)'s own service. Knowing when to use it and why, interviewers notice this immediately.

Cover Operational Performance.

This is the most underrated part of any HLD round.

Don't just explain how the system works.

Explain how it holds up under stress, traffic spikes, dependency failures, latency, observability.

One line I used in every HLD round,
"The system is designed to maintain acceptable latency and availability under adverse conditions such as traffic spikes, partial failures and dependency slowness using rate limiting, graceful degradation and observability."

This one line signals that you think like a production engineer, not just someone who read a tutorial.

All recently asked questions for [Amazon](https://linkedin.com/company/amazon) LLD, HLD and DSA are available on Codolio filtered by recency and popularity.

Link in comments. 👇

Anything specific you want me to go deeper on, drop it below. 🙂

# I interviewed at Google twice and Amazon once before finally cracking Amazon SDE 2. If I had to prepare in just 4 weeks, | Siddharth Singh · LinkedIn · 2026-07-10

**Siddharth Singh**: SDE 2 at Amazon for 5 months with 4 years 1 month of total professional experience. Previous roles include SDE 2 at Goldman Sachs, Software Engineer at Wells Fargo, and Program Associate at Wells Fargo. Based in Bengaluru, Karnataka, India [IN].

---

I interviewed at Google twice and Amazon once before finally cracking Amazon SDE 2. If I had to prepare in just 4 weeks,

This is exactly what I'd focus on.

- DSA

Don't try to solve random problems.
Focus on recently asked questions from the last 45 days and 6 months. That's what I did in my final 2 weeks.

You can find these directly on Codolio, filtered by company and recency.
(Link in comments👇)

Key patterns to cover:

→ Two Pointers - 3Sum, Sort Colors, Next Permutation
→ Sliding Window - Subarray Product Less Than K, Subarrays with K Different Integers
→ Binary Search - Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Koko Eating Bananas, Median of Two Sorted Arrays
→ Linked List - LRU Cache, LFU Cache, Merge k Sorted Lists, Copy List with Random Pointer
→ Stack - Trapping Rain Water, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Sum of Subarray Minimums
→ Trees - Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum, Lowest Common Ancestor, Vertical Order Traversal
→ Heap - Find Median from Data Stream, Task Scheduler
→ Backtracking - N-Queens, Combination Sum, Sudoku Solver
→ Graphs and DP - focus on patterns, not individual problems

One pro tip that saved me a lot of time,

You don't need to code every single problem. Read it, think of the approach, validate with the discussion section. Only code the ones where you genuinely feel you need to write it out.

I tracked every question I solved on Codolio, added notes on my approach, what I got wrong, what clicked. That revision habit made a big difference before the actual interview.

- Leadership Principles

Prepare all 16. Don't just prep the ones the recruiter mentioned.

Give ChatGPT your resume and full work experience as context. Ask it to draft STAR stories for each LP based on your actual experiences. Solid starting poin, then refine in your own words.

Fabricated answers always get caught in the follow-up questions so share real stories.

- Want the LLD and HLD breakdown too?

Comment "LLD" or "HLD" below and I'll cover it in the next post. 🙂

Amazon Interview Guide, Questions, Rounds and Pay (2026)

# The Amazon SDE Interview Guide

See how Amazon runs its software engineer loop: every round, what each one tests, and what each level pays. Then drill the real questions candidates report from recent loops, so nothing in the room catches you off guard.

- Loop length: 4 to 8 weeks
- Expected difficulty: Medium to hard
- Online assessment: CodeSignal
- System design: From SDE II

## Amazon levels & pay

- SDE I (L4, Entry)
- SDE II (L5, Mid)
- SDE III (L6, Senior)
- Principal SDE (L7, Principal)
- Senior Principal SDE (L8, Sr Principal)
- Distinguished Engineer (L10, Distinguished)

### Recruiter screen (30 to 45 min · call)

A short call with a recruiter, usually before anything technical happens. They walk through your resume, confirm which organization and team the role sits in, ask what level you are targeting, and check your timeline and pay expectations. It is rarely scored the way a real round is, but the level the recruiter writes down at the end shapes everything after it, because an SDE III loop is a genuinely different interview from an SDE II loop. This is also where they explain the Leadership Principles and tell you that behavioral questions run through every single round, which is a real instruction and worth taking literally. Amazon recruiters tend to answer direct questions directly, so use the time.

- Settle the level in this call. Ask which level the role is opened at and say which one you want. Changing level later normally means redoing rounds or accepting a down-level offer at the end, and both cost you weeks.
- Ask which organization the team sits in. AWS, Ads, Retail, Devices and the health and grocery businesses all run the same official loop but weight coding, distributed systems and operational depth differently. Knowing the org tells you what to practise.
- Give a range with a reason attached. Amazon works from bands and a level-specific cap on base pay, so a single number this early tends to become your ceiling. A range you can justify keeps the conversation open until you have an offer to negotiate against.

### Online assessment (2 to 3 hours · HackerRank)

A timed, auto-graded stage that you sit on your own, usually within about a week of getting the link, and normally delivered through HackerRank. In 2026 it is no longer coding only. Most candidates get two coding problems in roughly 70 to 90 minutes, then a work simulation of around 50 minutes, then a shorter work style survey, and some SDE II batches also get a short design-scenario module of about 20 minutes. The coding part carries the most weight and a weak score there is very hard to recover from, but Amazon reads the other parts as real signal too. Treat the whole thing as a round, because it filters you out before any human reads your resume.

- Hidden test cases decide your score. The grader runs cases you never see, so handling an empty input, a single element and an integer that overflows is worth more than tidy code. Spend the last five minutes walking your solution through the awkward inputs by hand.
- The work simulation is a simulated inbox. You get emails from a manager and two teammates, a log dump to read, a ticket to prioritize and an annoyed stakeholder to answer. It is scored against the Leadership Principles, so choose the option that digs into the actual data and tells people the bad news early.
- Answer the work style survey consistently. It is a situational judgment test with agree and disagree sliders, and it repeats the same underlying question in different wording to catch people guessing at what they think Amazon wants to hear. Answer as yourself, and answer the same way each time a question comes back around.

### Technical phone screen (45 to 60 min · shared editor)

One conversation with an Amazon engineer in a shared code editor, usually with no autocomplete and no way to run what you write. Not every candidate gets this round, since a strong OA sometimes goes straight to the loop, but most people sit it. You normally get one medium problem, sometimes two shorter ones, and at least one behavioral question mapped to a Leadership Principle inside the same hour. This is the first round where how you work is scored as heavily as what you produce, so working in silence hurts you even when the code is right. Most people who fail here fail on communication or on an edge case they never checked, and only rarely because the problem was beyond them.

- Ask about the input first. Size, ranges, duplicates, empty cases, whether it fits in memory. Two minutes of questions changes which solution is correct, and interviewers score whether you asked.
- Say the complexity out loud before you code. State the approach and its time and space cost, get a nod, then write it. Explaining only after the code is on screen is the most common way a technically fine candidate reads as unclear.
- Budget real time for the behavioral question. The interviewer has to fill in a Leadership Principle section on their written feedback whatever happens, so a story that arrives rushed in the last three minutes gets written up as thin. Leave ten minutes for it.

### The onsite loop (4 to 6 rounds · one day, virtual)

The main event, run as back-to-back interviews of about an hour each on a single day, usually virtual. For SDE II a typical shape is two coding rounds, one system design round, and one round that is either a low-level or object-oriented design problem or a third coding round depending on the team. SDE III and above shift weight towards design and ownership and lighten the pure algorithm load. Every round, including the design ones, also carries Leadership Principle questions, so you are scored on two axes in every single hour. One of these interviewers is the bar raiser, and you are usually not told which.

- Two coding rounds at medium to hard. The recurring areas are hash maps, trees, graphs with BFS and DFS, sliding window, heaps and intervals, with dynamic programming showing up more at senior levels. Interviewers expect the optimal time and space and expect you to handle edge cases without being prompted.
- System design from SDE II upward. You design one real service end to end: clarify what the customer actually needs, define the API, pick a data model, then work through scale, partitioning, caching and what happens when a component fails. Do the capacity arithmetic out loud, because being asked for a number and shrugging is a common way this round goes badly.
- Behavioral questions in every round, pushed several follow-ups deep. Bring one specific story per Leadership Principle with real numbers and your own actions in it, not the team's. Interviewers keep asking what happened next and who disagreed, so a story that ends where your preparation ends leaves you improvising in front of someone trained to notice.

### Debrief, bar raiser and offer (1 to 3 weeks after the loop)

After the loop every interviewer writes up detailed feedback with examples before they see anyone else's, and the debrief cannot be booked until all of it is filed. The bar raiser is a trained interviewer from outside the hiring team whose job is to protect the long-term hiring bar rather than to fill this role, and they lead the discussion and can effectively veto a hire the team wants. Because the decision is argued from written evidence, a round where you were fine but unmemorable reads as weak on paper. An even loop across every round is what clears the bar, and one standout round sitting next to one thin one usually stalls here. If the group thinks you are strong but not at the level you interviewed for, the usual outcome is a down-level offer rather than a rejection.

- Every claim in the room is backed by a quote or an example. Interviewers write down what you actually said, so a vague story with no numbers in it cannot be defended by anyone in the debrief even if the interviewer liked you.
- The bar raiser weighs Leadership Principle signal heavily. A loop with clean code and thin behavioral evidence stalls here more often than people expect, particularly at SDE II and above where ownership and judgment are the level definition.
- Expect one to three weeks, then a separate pay conversation. The debrief itself usually happens within about a week of the loop and the decision follows within another few days, then offer approval and negotiation add several more. Hiring pauses and reschedules stretch this, so ask your recruiter for a date rather than guessing.

### Keep a daily coding rhythm (Weeks 1 to 4)

Code every day for the whole month. Rotate through the patterns Amazon leans on, hash maps, trees, graphs and BFS, sliding window, and heaps, starting at medium and climbing into hard as the weeks go on, always timed on a shared editor.

### Prepare a story for every Leadership Principle (Weeks 1 to 2)

Draft these early so you have three weeks to rehearse them. Write one specific STAR example for each of the 16 principles, each with concrete metrics and your role, and practice delivering each in about two minutes.

### Layer in system-design reps (Weeks 2 to 3)

Once your coding is warm, add system design (SDE II and up) alongside it. Work through three or four full designs end to end, scoping, API, data model, scaling, and capacity math, saying each decision aloud and preparing for follow-ups on your trade-offs.

### Run full mock loops (Week 4)

In the last week, put it all together: sit a few complete loops back to back, coding, system design, and behavioral in one session each, so your focus and answers hold across four or five interviews in a row.

Design an LRU cache with per-key TTL and O(1) operations

## About Amazon

Amazon operates across three segments, North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). Engineering hires span retail, devices, advertising, and the AWS cloud, and the bar centers on scalable systems, ownership, and the Leadership Principles.

Because so much of Amazon runs on AWS-scale infrastructure, the SDE loop leans on practical distributed-systems thinking and a values bar that carries genuine weight, more than pure algorithm speed.

### How many rounds is the Amazon interview?

Typically five stages: a recruiter screen, an online assessment, a technical phone screen, and a virtual onsite of four to five rounds. Every technical round also includes Leadership Principle questions.

### How hard is the Amazon SDE interview?

Medium to hard. Of the questions Karavine tracks, about 36 percent rate hard, concentrated in graph problems and system design. The coding bar is beatable with focused pattern practice; the system-design round decides most senior loops.

### What is the Amazon online assessment (OA)?

A timed, auto-graded stage with coding problems and, for some roles, a work-style survey and work simulation. It filters before the phone screen, so treat it as a real round, not a formality.

### What are the Amazon Leadership Principles in interviews?

Sixteen principles, Ownership, Dive Deep, Bias for Action, Deliver Results, and more, that behavioral questions map to. Prepare one specific STAR story per principle with metrics and your exact role.

### Does Amazon ask system design?

Yes, from SDE II and up, weighted more heavily at senior levels. Expect a full design: API, data model, scaling, caching, failure handling, and capacity math you can defend under follow-ups.

### What is the Amazon SDE II (L5) salary?

Median total compensation for an SDE II is about $270k a year in Seattle, made up of roughly $178k base plus around $90k a year of RSUs, with a modest target bonus. Amazon vests 5/15/40/40, so year one pays far less than a flat quarter of the grant, and the year-1 and year-2 sign-on bonuses exist to bridge exactly that gap.
